US stocks have lost an average of $225 billion per day for 31 consecutive trading days.

Below, we systematically outline how things got to this point, what is happening now, and what we are about to see.

Since November 2022, we have been highly optimistic about AI, calling it the biggest technological revolution in history.

Our "either hold the assets or be left behind" judgment was based on innovation-driven returns and ever-accumulating inflation.

Over the past six weeks, AI trading has faced one of its most severe tests since its inception, comparable to the challenges during the trade war in April 2025. The reality is that AI is disrupting the existing order of global markets, economies, and civilization. This disruption will lead to emotional polarization, which will only be amplified by significant asset price volatility. And this is precisely what we are seeing right now.

data.title: A dangerous cycle in the AI ​​computing power market: the harder it is to borrow money, the more expensive GPU rentals become.
data.description:
Author: Li Jia, Wall Street Insights

Lending institutions tightened financing for NeoCloud, reducing the loan-to-value ratio from 80% to 50%-60%, forcing buyers to turn to the spot market, which in turn pushed up GPU rental prices. Rising rental prices supported GPU asset valuations, but startups still rely on venture capital for computing power procurement, while token prices continued to fall. This could create a vicious cycle between tightened financing and fragile demand.

The continued surge in GPU rental prices may not be due to strong demand for AI computing power, but rather to a supply contraction caused by tightened financing channels.

Stanley Lee, Chief Product Officer of Liquid Compute, recently pointed out on the Odd Lots podcast that current GPU spot and short-term rental prices reflect capital costs more than changes in underlying demand.

Lenders tightening financing terms for mid-sized new cloud service providers (like Neocloud) are forcing buyers unable to secure long-term loans to turn to the short-term spot market, thus driving up visible rents. The change in financing terms is already quite evident. Lenders' loan-to-value (LTV) ratio for Neocloud has fallen from 80% this summer to the current 50% to 60%. Meanwhile, CoreWeave credit default swap (CDS) spreads have widened to approximately 1300 basis points, and its 2031 bond yield has risen to 16%. Rich Privorotsky, head of trading at Goldman Sachs, previously called GPU rents the single most important indicator in AI trading, but Goldman Sachs now acknowledges that while spot rents are supported by physical scarcity, the underlying economics are deteriorating. The real question is: is the rent increase stemming from customer business growth or from purchasing power generated by the previous round of equity financing? Tighter Credit Drives Up GPU Rentals: Financing Difficulties Lead to Higher Spot Prices GPU rentals have seen a significant increase recently. Silicon Data's B200 index rose 23.5% from the end of August to November 19, from $5.62 per GPU hour to $6.94, briefly reaching $7.10 on Tuesday. H100 rentals have increased 67% since July 2025. Dell founder Michael Dell also stated last week that H100 hourly rentals have risen from $1.96 a year ago to $3.10. However, behind the rising rentals, financing thresholds are rapidly increasing. Stanley Lee stated that mid-sized neoclouds typically use GPUs as collateral to obtain hundreds of millions of dollars in fully amortized loans over three years, relying on take-or-pay contracts signed with AI customers for repayment. This summer, the LTV (Lifetime Value) of such loans reached as high as 80%, dropping to 70% after Labor Day. Currently, lenders generally require a reduction to 50% to 60%, with interest rates for 50% LTV loans already at a mid-to-high level of over ten percentage points. For example, for a $100 million GPU cluster, the funds neoclouds need to raise themselves have increased from $30 million to a maximum of $50 million, an increase of approximately 67%. Previously, many small operators relied on customer prepayments to fill funding gaps; now, they are forced to request additional prepayments from customers or turn to equity financing. Tighter financing has directly altered market supply and demand: operators are finding it difficult to obtain long-term loans, slowing down the construction of new clusters; buyers unable to sign long-term contracts are turning to the short-term spot market, driving up rents. Even without increased end-user demand, this process is enough to drive up rental prices. Startups prefer to pay higher rents rather than pay upfront. Fundraising pressures have also changed the way AI startups procure resources. Lee cites an example: a customer faces two B300 computing power leasing plans: one at $4.40 per GPU hour with a 30% down payment; the other with no down payment but an hourly rate of approximately $5.65. The customer often prefers the latter. Based on a three-year, 24-hour plan, the former would cost approximately $115,600 in total, with a down payment of approximately $34,700; the latter would cost approximately $148,500 in total. To save upfront capital, customers need to pay an additional $33,000, implying an annualized financing cost of approximately 30% to 55%. This choice reflects the financial difficulties faced by startups: cash reserves are often more important than financing costs. Preserving cash can extend operating time, while increasing computing power helps scale the business, drive revenue growth, and create conditions for the next round of venture capital funding. However, this also means that rising GPU rental costs do not necessarily indicate stronger profitability for customers; some demand is still actually supported by external equity financing. Rising rental costs do not equate to strong demand: market prices deviate from actual value. GPU leasing market pricing is not uniform. In analyzing CoreWeave's claim that idle GPU subleasing could generate $10 billion in revenue annually, Bernstein listed H100 quotes from four vendors on the same day: $3.50, $3.30, $3.01, and $2.80 per hour, a 25% difference between the highest and lowest, while CoreWeave management assumed a price of $3.81. Ornn's H100 index has also fallen from around $3.50 in early November to $2.92. Lee warns that if the rent increase is due to harder access to credit rather than increased end-user demand, then this market is unhealthy. Once financing channels further tighten and operators run out of cash, market prices could fall rapidly. Private lending firms have begun to pay attention to this risk. In the past two weeks, Liquid Compute has received one to three calls daily from large private lending funds inquiring about put options on the B300 leasing index, whereas six months ago there was almost no such demand. Meanwhile, large neocloud companies are also inquiring about acquiring GPU clusters when smaller competitors are selling assets at a discount. More alarmingly, while GPU rental costs are rising, the price of computing power output is falling. Since July, Ornn's OpenAI token price index has dropped from over $1.20 to $0.31, and the Anthropic index has fallen from approximately $2 to $0.77. Nvidia also stated on Tuesday that token prices have fallen by nearly 60% since May. Rising input costs and falling output prices are squeezing the profit margins of computing power operators. After the retreat of venture capital, GPU rental costs may see a reversal. The core concern regarding current AI computing power demand is that buyers' ability to pay remains highly dependent on venture capital. Lee points out that the key to judging whether computing power demand is sustainable lies in whether customers can shift from equity financing to using business revenue to pay for computing power bills. Aside from a few companies like Anthropic, there is currently a lack of sufficient publicly available data to prove that this shift has already occurred. Rothschild Redburn analyst Alexander Haissl previously pointed out that while computing power prices for companies like CoreWeave and Nebius have increased, the highest bidders are often venture-backed startups, and the sustainability of their demand depends on the continued injection of external capital. Nvidia has consistently been a significant source of funding in this financing system, but its interim CEO, Colette Kress, stated on Tuesday that Nvidia will continue to support neocloud while adopting more prudent selection criteria. The scale of financing is also not to be underestimated. Goldman Sachs' credit strategy team predicts that chip and computing power financing will reach $320 billion in 2027, nearly seven times this year's level. Podcast guest Paul Kedrosky warned that while the current AI investment system is expanding rapidly, the contraction could be far faster than expected should the funding chain reverse. The danger lies in the possibility that if venture capital slows down and customers stop paying, operators may default, and the GPU clusters repossessed by lenders will re-enter the market. At that point, new supply will coincide with weakening demand, and the current rents driven up by tightening credit could quickly reverse.

data.title: Galaxy: How do you view the impact of the Anthropic IPO on market liquidity?
data.description:
Author: Alex Thorn, Head of Research at Galaxy; Translator: Gu Yu, ChainCatcher

This weekend saw heightened market sentiment, coinciding with Anthropic's Nasdaq IPO.

Anthropic completed the largest IPO in history on Wednesday evening, pricing its offering at $83 per share. When the company updated its prospectus last week, it had projected a price range of $70 to $78. Strong demand prompted the AI ​​company, best known for its Claude chatbot, to expand its offering, selling approximately 980 million shares and raising $81.3 billion, up from the initially planned 825 million shares. This figure surpasses the $75 billion raised by Musk's SpaceX in its June IPO, and Anthropic's IPO pricing means the barely six-year-old company is valued at approximately $1.5 trillion.

Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley led the deal, just as they did with SpaceX. Before the market opened, Cboe's JJ Kinahan said demand was almost seven times the offering size, and CNBC sources reported retail demand was the largest in history. The stock began trading on Nasdaq at 11:48 a.m. ET on Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT. The first trade was at $111.50, 34% above the IPO price, briefly giving the company a market capitalization of $2 trillion. The stock hit an intraday high of $114.99 within a minute of the first trade, before steadily declining for the remainder of the session. As of 2:18 p.m. ET, the stock was trading at $94.67, in the mid-range of $90, up about 14% from the offering price. The decline from the opening price was unusually steep. According to Yahoo Finance, of the 20 major U.S. IPOs since 2008, only Coupang performed worse at the same point on its first day; the group averaged a gain of about 3.5%. The broader market also saw a sell-off after the stock opened. As soon as Anthropic began trading, the stock market fell to its intraday low, with chip stocks, including Nvidia and Broadcom, erasing their gains. Listed ANT options are scheduled to begin trading on Monday. On the blockchain, Hyperliquid once again demonstrated the success of its pre-IPO perpetual contract market. Its market accurately predicted the trading price: perpetual contracts traded well above the $70-$78 range for weeks, indicating stronger demand than the underwriters' initial targets. The perpetual contract ultimately closed about 7% lower than the opening price, with the contract price at approximately $103.67 at 8:40 AM ET, about 25% higher than the offering price of $83 per share. Thursday morning's perpetual contract price largely aligned with market consensus (Cboe's Kinahan suggested the first trade should have been around $103 or $104), but both the perpetual contract and market professionals ultimately misjudged, with the first trade ending at $111.50. However, the perpetual contract accurately captured the stock's final trading position. For most of the period before the listing, the perpetual contract traded in the mid-to-high range of $90. It was around $96.93 as of November 17th, and $98.83 on the hourly chart the night before pricing, having briefly dipped below $94 during the earlier tech stock sell-off. After opening higher and then falling back, the stock returned to this range, trading in the afternoon between approximately $94 and $97. It could be argued that the perpetual contract's week-long equilibrium price better estimated the "fair" value of the first day than the opening price, which appeared to be a temporary spike in demand. Our Views It's a strange feeling to watch Anthropic employees applaud on the Nasdaq trading floor as they celebrate the IPO of a company whose major media narrative is that AI could kill us all. This week has been one of the most apocalyptic in recent memory, with the backdrop of Microsoft O365 outages on Thursday, a nationwide FAA grounding on Friday, banking system disruptions on Monday, and even reported interference with the NSA's internal communications systems (twice?). Costco reported a wave of panic buying, people withdrew cash from banks, and doomsday preparedness content went viral on social media. Discussions among traders ranged from which solar cells to buy, how to store large quantities of dry food in a New York City apartment, to the best routes to escape the city in the event of a grid failure. Therefore, including "the end of humanity" in the S-1 risk factors for this week's sensational IPO might not be more fitting. (While we are not stock analysts, we agree that the end of humanity could have a substantial impact on Anthropic's earnings.) Since October 1st, the S&P 500 has fallen 7%, gold 12.2%, and BTC 25%. US Treasury bonds are depreciating, inflation is high, interest rates are expected to rise, commodities are falling, and Democrats came to power primarily on calls to address the "affordability crisis." Our own Bitcoin Fear & Greed Index is near all-time lows (meaning "extreme fear"), and the VIX is trading at levels comparable to those during the March Iran war, though not yet at the levels seen during the April 2025 "tariff farce." Stanley Druckenmiller stated that he is "more uncertain than ever after 50 years of investing," and his firm's equity positions are "basically flat." Another Wall Street figure, Howard Marks, argued in a November 11 memo titled "A Layman's Thoughts on AI" that the astonishing speed of AI development is a significant risk, even for Anthropic. Paul Tudor Jones stated in mid-October, "2027 is going to be a very tough year for the stock market." Therefore, it's fair to say that the stock market intellectual community is uneasy. Some speculate that the recent headwinds facing risk assets have been exacerbated by the liquidity drain caused by investors withdrawing assets to purchase Anthropic's IPO. This does make sense intuitively, but there isn't much direct evidence to support this claim. Bitcoin's price action mirrored its weak performance ahead of the SpaceX IPO in June, hitting a bear market low on July 1st (US$57,717 on Coinbase). Whether BTC and other risk assets will get a breather after ANT becomes a publicly traded company remains to be seen. The reality is that Americans are fearful and psychologically traumatized. Polarization has long been a feature of the American political landscape, but the Democratic Party's overwhelming victory was so dramatic that significant shifts in tax policy, AI policy, and legislative priorities are expected. Coupled with the endless drumbeats about cyber vulnerabilities and the broad spectrum of AI outcomes—ranging from the possibility of permanent utopia to the possibility of species extinction—it's easy to understand why the market is volatile. There's a sense that just one more major piece of bad news could push the market to the brink—a major cyberattack, an escalation of the war in Iran or Ukraine, a pandemic, or a major natural disaster. On the other hand, a major peace agreement or initiative resulting from Trump's meetings with Xi Jinping and Putin, a halt to major regional conflicts, or a legislative breakthrough in Congress could alleviate these fears. As people say, if you're going through hell, just keep going. The only way out is to get through. Everything is different now, yes, but everything is alright. Bitcoin continues to produce blocks without interruption, and I've just written a clever new dashboard to monitor the situation. —Alex Thorn

For other risks related to digital assets, please refer to the risk factors set out in Galaxy Digital Inc.'s filings with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC”) from time to time, including its Form 10-Q quarterly reports, available at www.sec.gov.

data.title: Is the era of easy money in the crypto industry over? Four common tricks are draining market liquidity.
data.description:
Author: Paul Klay; Translation: AididiaoJP, Foresight News

The crypto market has seen a recurring pattern of various schemes over the past few years. I believe these have played a key role in "why there are almost no more easy ways to make money like before," and those opportunities are unlikely to return.

I'm not talking about Bitcoin prices or trading volumes, nor am I a crypto analyst; the following are just my personal opinions.

Easy money is only possible when others are willing to spend money. The vast majority of crypto market participants are gamblers. Of course, there are real technologies and practical use cases, but those who participate in everything and treat crypto as a full-time job are, to some extent, gamblers.

So, as long as you're a little smarter than others, get information earlier, and then sell it to later investors, who eventually sell it to retail investors, you can make money. Even if you're not the earliest entrant, there are still considerable opportunities to make money.

Most of these people, after making money, immediately reinvest it back into crypto.

Just like in a casino, they move their money to other opportunities they think will earn more. This all happens relatively organically. Everyone makes money, and everyone loses money. No single group consistently takes all the profits. We know that in traditional casinos, the casino owner is the one who makes the money. So several groups decide to become casino owners themselves. They figure out ways to profit from all the fluctuations and take that money out of the market. The best part for them is that in the casinos they create, there's almost no chance of losing money. They're simply exploiting people's greed. Below, I'll discuss what I believe are the four biggest and most common tactics that play a decisive role. Trump and Insider Trading Trump recognized his enormous opportunity to influence crypto and the stock market and actively used it. Crypto is the focus here because it's smaller, less volatile, and more easily manipulated. When you're in control of the market, you and those around you have a huge informational advantage. The strategy is simple: determine which direction is more profitable, build a position, and make as much profit as market liquidity allows. Keep doing this until people stop believing you, stop reacting to your statements, or there's no more liquidity to be drawn. The problem is, markets aren't infinite. There are a limited number of gamblers, and their money is limited. When insiders use their market influence, they can siphon off huge sums of money, concentrating wealth in the hands of a small group who may not necessarily reinvest it in crypto. Furthermore, Trump and his family issued several tokens, but that's another matter. Therefore, the victory the crypto community celebrated during the election may ultimately become its worst nightmare. Cryptocrime is essentially the same idea, except you're not influencing prices because you're the US president, but because you control a large portion of the token supply and your coin has futures trading on major exchanges. The steps are as follows: create a project, raise funds from well-known investors, use that money to boost trading volume and followers, showcase non-existent revenue, raise another round, and negotiate a listing on a major exchange.

If you can get futures trading immediately, great. If not, keep increasing volume until you can.

Now you have a machine that looks like it can print money infinitely.

When there is futures trading and you control most of the supply, you can monitor how many people are shorting and how many are going long. You choose the side that is favorable to you, buy or sell enough to trigger the other side's collapse, and then take the profits.

Repeat as many times as possible until the token is delisted or the scheme fails.

To operate on a large scale, you need to have futures trading on a large exchange, because that's where the trading volume comes from.

No matter how good a project is in reality, as long as the token has futures on Binance, it can attract hundreds of millions of dollars in trading volume. Projects with severely inflated valuations that are completely mismatched with their revenue. Crypto is still a relatively young industry, and projects often receive very high valuation multiples. Many people don't really understand what others are talking about. Countless projects with advanced technology and grand visions are normal. Like other industries, most projects with flawed assumptions eventually shut down, and a few drive the market forward. But crypto has two key differences: How revenue is generated. Because of the nature of the market—most people come looking for easy ways to make money—and because of how many founders and marketers position projects, ultimately almost everyone's real motivation is to make money, not to solve problems. Founders encourage users to use the technology by promising potential rewards through airdrops. People do use it, but not because the technology solves their problems, but because they expect to make money. Founders use these metrics to attract investors, raise huge sums of money, and eventually issue a token. After distributing rewards to users, activity sometimes drops hundreds or even thousands of times because people are only using the product in anticipation of financial rewards. Token issuance. In other industries, projects that fail shut down. Investors lose money, and founders waste time. But in crypto, even if the idea completely fails, weaker regulation and oversight can allow you to continue claiming everything is fine, constructing a compelling narrative, and issuing tokens at severely inflated valuations completely unrelated to the project's actual value. And people will buy. Founders make money, and investors either recoup some of their investment, sometimes even making a profit, even though the project should have shut down. This is essentially an IPO without equivalent regulation or meaningful due diligence. You can list whenever you want, pay to get listed on an exchange, and that's it. The level of scrutiny can be surprisingly low. A colleague of mine created a product I really like, @valueverse_ai, which compares actual revenue with valuation to identify undervalued projects. This helps explain why so many crypto tokens list with declining charts, with a few exceptions, sometimes due to manipulation rather than genuine demand. Meanwhile, many projects that truly generate real revenue don't even issue tokens. Returning to market fundamentals, this model works when new players are constantly entering the market. But theoretically, it simply cannot function in the long run if it doesn't create real value. Everyone wants to make money, but someone has to lose money. So founders start mass-producing projects, using token issuance as a way to exit liquidity. I know many teams are issuing tokens, and they're still doing it, several projects a week. Imagine that. Several projects every week. They just package them, fake attractive metrics, pay influencers to promote them, and then pocket the profits. Runaways. In the previous example, we were talking about severely inflated valuations. A project that should be worth $10 million by all metrics was valued at $1 billion. Here, it's just mass-issuing meme tokens. Many teams are doing this. The probability of them losing money is extremely low because they control the supply and can dump their holdings. Even if only one out of 100 tokens takes off, they can still make a fortune. That's it. Similarly, no real value is created. You're simply given an opportunity to satisfy your gambling instincts, just like in a casino. The difference is that traditional casinos sometimes lose money in the short term. Here, operators can arrange things with almost no downside risk. And your odds might be worse than in a casino. As a result, the market is increasingly shifting towards institutional players and products with real use cases. A compelling story alone no longer works as well as it used to, and most of the easy money opportunities that come with it are no longer effective. You could say the industry has matured, and I agree. But at the same time, with a relatively small group of people siphoning huge sums of money from it, the market doesn't feel like it did in its early days. This is inevitable because the model was fundamentally unsustainable from the start. At the same time, I believe this industry has enormous potential, and I'm confident it will continue to grow in the long term, just not in the same way as before. Previously, the industry was full of extremely incompetent people who built ecosystems but had no concept of how to run a business, yet everyone was paying them. They then hired some of the most unqualified experts I've ever seen, paying them the highest salaries I've ever seen. Most of those people have now left, which is a good thing. Money is no longer being given to everyone for no reason. This creates an incentive to build real businesses that solve real problems. And this should ultimately have a very positive impact on the industry.

data.title: Has the greatest challenge in mathematics been conquered? Anthropic claims to have proven the Riemann Hypothesis.
data.description:
Author: Li Jia, Wall Street Insights

The Riemann Hypothesis, which has puzzled the mathematical community for 167 years, may see its first major breakthrough, but whether the AI-generated proof can withstand the scrutiny of the mathematical community remains the biggest suspense.

On November 20th, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge announced that he and the AI ​​model Claude had found a proof method for the Riemann Hypothesis and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH), and simultaneously released over 17 million lines of Lean formal code. Since the announcement coincided with the day after Anthropic's IPO, this mathematical breakthrough has sparked discussions about the timing of the release and the commercial motives.

Alpöge released the proof in Lean, divided into 14 compressed files. At the same time, the text version of the proof generated by him and Claude exceeded 250,000 pages, but it was not made public due to its excessive length and difficulty in reading.

Currently, no scientists have officially confirmed the validity of this proof. Further verification is needed to confirm whether the theorems ultimately proven by the Lean code truly correspond to the Riemann Hypothesis itself, and whether there are any logical flaws in the entire proof process.

Riemann's classic portrait (1850s)

Proof method: Claude achieves a key breakthrough at the "finish line"

250,000-page proof: The contradiction between AI breakthrough and human verification

The sheer length of the proof has become another focus of attention in the mathematics community.

Thomas Bloom, a mathematician at the University of Manchester, stated on X that he didn't know whether he was more shocked by AI's claim of proving the Riemann Hypothesis or by its claim of generating a logically coherent proof exceeding 250,000 pages in human-readable form.

Pierre Richemond, head of Cohere's multimodal business and former Google DeepMind researcher, believes that the Riemann Hypothesis may have been solved, but still awaits Lean's verification. This progress raises more questions: AI-generated research results already possess serious mathematical value, but have not yet undergone sufficient verification by the human mathematical community.

Timing Controversy: Announced the Day After IPO, Alpöge Responds Proactively

The timing of the statement's release also attracted attention. Anthropic went public on November 19th, and Alpöge's announcement of this major mathematical breakthrough the following day inevitably sparked speculation about his commercial motives.

Alpöge proactively addressed this controversy in his statement, acknowledging that "the precise timing was terrible." He stated that the key work was completed late on November 15th to early on November 16th local time, after which he asked Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei whether it could be made public, "and ultimately we figured out that there were indeed restrictions to follow."

Alpöge proactively addressed this controversy in his statement, acknowledging that "the precise timing was terrible."

... He denied negative speculation about the release date, calling such "obvious cynical views" wrong, and stated that he "couldn't wait any longer" and was willing to take full responsibility. It's worth noting that Anthropic had previously made progress in AI mathematics research. In August of this year, the company announced Claude's research results on the distribution of zeros in the Riemann zeta function, raising the lower bound of the proportion of zeros on the critical line from 41.6% to 67.2%. However, at the time, Anthropic explicitly stated that it did not expect the technology used by Claude to ultimately prove the Riemann Hypothesis.

Prize and Recognition: Still Years Away from the Millennium Prize

Even if the proof is ultimately valid, Alpöge is still quite far from the $1 million prize established by the Clay Mathematics Institute.

According to the institute's rules, a solution to the Millennium Prize Problem must be formally published, undergo at least two years of public scrutiny, and gain widespread international recognition from the mathematical community before it can be eligible for the prize.

Alpöge himself is optimistic about the form the proof will take once it is finally accepted. He believes that the proof will likely be significantly simplified and may be realized very soon. He describes this progress as "a dawn of something greater in the field of science."

When you simplify complex real-world problems into a single-dimensional number in pursuit of mathematical measurability, you easily fall into the trap of the blind men and the elephant.

For example, funding mosquito nets to prevent malaria is extremely easy to quantify in terms of cost and short-term benefits; however, funding institutional development, breakthroughs in basic science, or the prevention of civilizational catastrophes has long-term impacts that are full of unquantifiable parameters in mathematical models. To abandon those far-reaching attempts that truly determine the fate of civilization simply because they cannot be precisely quantified is itself the greatest betrayal of rationality. Eli Goldfine: Does this mean that excessive quantification has become a dogmatic trap of effective altruism? Sam Bankman-Fried: Indeed. When people are overly obsessed with the verifiability of mathematical models, they instinctively reject truly disruptive but uncertain grand propositions. A healthy evaluation framework must acknowledge the boundaries of human cognition and maintain a dynamic balance between quantitative precision and intuitive perspective.

51/49 The Extreme Philosophical Question of a Coin Toss: Pure Expectation Value vs. Irreversible Destruction and Diminishing Margins

Eli Goldfine: I'd like to discuss a well-known thought experiment with you. Economist Tyler Cowen once posed a hypothetical question to you: If there's a coin, heads has a 51% probability of doubling the overall utility of the Earth, and tails has a 49% probability of causing the complete destruction of the Earth, would you choose to toss the coin? At the time, your answer was yes. Today, in prison, do you still adhere to this pure expectation value logic?

Sam Bankman-Fried: This is a classic debate topic that is extremely fascinating in philosophy and probability theory.

If you strictly limit the problem to purely mathematical assumptions and a linear expected utility function, the mathematical answer is obvious: 51% multiplied by 2 is greater than 1, the expected value is positive, and any staunch expectancy maximizer must logically accept this gamble. However, in the real world, this thought experiment is instinctively rejected by most normal people because it ignores fundamental constraints in the real world that cannot be simply abstracted. Eli Goldfine: What exactly are these ignored real-world constraints? Sam Bankman-Fried: First, destruction is absolutely irreversible (Catastrophic Ruin). In a game of probability, if you have a certain probability of going to zero and permanently exiting the game, you will never have the chance to enjoy the benefits of subsequent positive expected values. Second, utility is never strictly linear; it suffers from strong diminishing marginal utility. In reality, the increased happiness brought to human civilization by doubling Earth's utility is far from offsetting the infinite suffering caused by a 49% probability of complete annihilation. Applying an extreme model stripped of diminishing marginal utility and bankruptcy protection directly to the real world often leads to extremely dangerous judgment biases. Eli Goldfine: If delaying technological development could result in a lower probability of destruction, would you support slowing down? Sam Bankman-Fried: If, in a theoretical model, delaying humanity's entry into superintelligence by a hundred years could reduce the probability of civilization's destruction by even just 1%, then from the macroscopic long-term perspective of the universe's future billions of years, this hundred-year stagnation is mathematically worthwhile. Because the future of the universe is infinitely long, and once civilization reaches zero, it is completely finished. High-expectation-value games in reality: If you were to gamble 51/49 on personal freedom, would you give it up? Eli Goldfine: What if this gamble were replaced with real-world stakes that directly affect you? Suppose you have a coin toss where there's a 51% chance you'll be released from prison immediately tomorrow without charge, and a 49% chance your sentence will double or you'll even be sentenced to death. Would you flip the coin? Sam Bankman-Fried: This vividly illustrates why utility functions in reality aren't linear. When it comes to core assets like personal freedom and life, people's aversion to extreme downside risks is immense. If I were released tomorrow, my life would undoubtedly improve dramatically; but if the cost is a nearly 50% chance of enduring a longer or even fatal abyss, that risk premium is unacceptable. This is why complex decisions in reality should never be made hastily based on a rough expected value. Eli Goldfine: Many people believe that your past investment and business decisions were products of this philosophy of extreme expectations. Do you agree with this assessment? Sam Bankman-Fried: I think the outside world has oversimplified my thinking. In regular trading, we pay extreme attention to hedging and risk exposure management; however, in the event of an extreme crisis, the safety cushion of many theoretical models can be instantly punctured. The real world is not a Monte Carlo simulation in an ivory tower; the destructive power of black swans far exceeds the expectations of mathematical equations. Final Question: Was it all really worth it? Decision-making distortions and winner narratives in crisis. Eli Goldfine: We only have a few minutes left. I want to ask a very soul-searching question: Considering the shocking collapse of FTX, but at the same time, the FTX Future Fund funded a massive number of cutting-edge technology and security projects, including Anthropic, in its early stages. Looking back at the whole ordeal, was it really worth it on a macro level? Sam Bankman-Fried: No. I'd love to give a self-deceptive yes, but I can't honestly say it was. I think it should have been. If I hadn't messed things up at the last minute, if those risk defenses hadn't crumbled, it could have been a huge force driving the world forward. Perhaps it retains some cautionary value if future generations can learn the right lessons from this disaster, but in reality, most people aren't learning anything. Eli Goldfine: What are the real lessons people should learn? Sam Bankman-Fried: The core lesson is just one: how distorted the decisions people make in extreme panic when a crisis truly arrives and the situation is completely out of control. Under the pressure of life and death, people lose their judgment about what truly matters at an alarming rate, and all rules crumble in an instant. And after the dust settles, history is always written by the victors. The causal details of every event are reshaped, distorted, and simplified through the victor's lens. For those outside the storm, it's virtually impossible to penetrate the fog of the victor's narrative to uncover the true mechanisms. A survival guideline for the new generation of 14-year-olds: Stop doing quantitative trading on Wall Street, dedicate yourself to AI. Eli Goldfine: As a 14-year-old facing the coming era of superintelligence, what is your core advice for me if I want to create the greatest positive value in this world? Sam Bankman-Fried: Ten years ago, the standard answer from the effective altruistic community would have been "Earning to Give": go to Wall Street, do high-frequency trading, make billions of dollars, and then donate the wealth to charity. But times have completely changed. At this juncture approaching the singularity, high-frequency trading on Wall Street is no longer the most important battleground. The window between now and the full-fledged takeoff of AI is narrowing rapidly, and the value of deeply understanding and harnessing machine intelligence is rising exponentially. Whether it's dedicating yourself to cutting-edge AI alignment and security research, or finding a piece of traditional infrastructure and fully automating it with AI, delving into the core of machine intelligence is the only truly worthwhile battleground in this era.

data.title: Four checks a week: The printing press slows down as Tether begins investing.
data.description:
Author: Daisy, Deep Tide TechFlow

From November 16th to 19th, Tether signed four checks in four days.

The first was in Brazil, where Tether Capital led the Series C round for USD account service provider Nomad, investing $15 million, bringing the total round to 172 million reais and valuing the company at 4 billion reais post-money.

The second was for Stables, a payment infrastructure company that processes over $2 billion in USDT transactions annually, focusing on Asia and the Middle East and North Africa.

The third was in Singapore, where Tether and Abu Dhabi's Further Asset Management jointly invested approximately $10 million in MetaComp.

The fourth transaction was in Switzerland, targeting SCRYPT, one of the largest stablecoin trading and liquidity providers in the country. All four companies are doing the same thing: facilitating the flow of US dollars across borders. Two weeks before signing these checks, Tether had just released its third-quarter report. The printing press has slowed down. As of September 30, Tether had $191.5 billion in reserve assets, including $132.4 billion in US Treasury bonds, and a net operating profit of $4.5 billion for the first nine months of this year. While these figures still seem large, Tether's net profit for the first three quarters of the same period last year had already exceeded $10 billion. The statistical methods used in the two years are different; last year, net profit was reported, while this year, net operating profit is reported, so they cannot be directly subtracted. The profits for the first three quarters of this year were $1.04 billion, $1.5 billion, and $1.5 billion, respectively. At this rate, it will be difficult to return to the high point of over $13 billion in 2024 for the whole year. More importantly, another figure is that the issuance of USDT in the first three quarters of this year has basically stopped at $184 billion. Tether's business can be broken down into a multiplication, that is, the circulating scale of USDT multiplied by the yield on US Treasury bonds. For every $1 deposited by a user, Tether uses it to buy short-term US Treasury bonds to earn interest. The Federal Reserve began cutting interest rates in the fall of 2024, and the yield variable has been declining; this year, the scale variable has also remained unchanged. With both variables stuck, profits can only fall. Tether can't control interest rates; all it can do is push the scale back up. Relying on the existing cryptocurrency holdings on exchanges to support the next $100 billion is unrealistic. New scale can only come from real wages, payments, remittances, and daily bills outside the cryptocurrency sphere. To absorb this money, there needs to be a channel. Instead of teaching users, it directly invests in the channels. Tether realized early on that it's virtually impossible to teach everyone in the world how to download wallets, write mnemonic phrases, and calculate on-chain transaction fees. So it simply stopped teaching and directly invested in the financial apps that users were already using. This strategy began to take shape in 2024. In April of that year, Tether restructured into four major sectors: Data, Finance, Power, and Edu, and its investments began to have clear industry objectives. In June of the same year, it invested $18.75 million in Taipei-based XREX, specifically for compliant USDT cross-border B2B payments, serving SMEs in emerging markets. Subsequently, the checkbook expanded along the map of high inflation, foreign exchange controls, and remittance demand. In Africa, in October 2025, Tether invested in Kenya's Kotani Pay, a company that integrates blockchain applications with mobile wallets and local banking systems across Africa. In Latin America, in April, it led a $14 million Series A funding round for the Argentine crypto-finance platform Belo; in July, it invested $20 million in Mercado Bitcoin, a Brazilian on-chain financial platform serving 4.5 million users, and also disclosed a $20 million stake in the funding round for the Argentine digital bank Ualá. The Ualá investment best illustrates Tether's intentions. This bank has over 11 million customers, but due to local regulatory restrictions, USDT will not be integrated in the short term. Tether is still investing. Even if integration is not possible immediately, it will still acquire shares, and when regulations ease, it will already be on the shareholder list. The same applies to Nomad, which was signed this week. Nomad has 3.8 million customers and manages approximately 8 billion reais in assets. The integration of USDT and the gold token XAUT is still in the exploratory stage, and no launch date has been announced. However, these customers were already holding US dollars, so Tether saved several years' worth of customer acquisition costs. Brazil is also one of the most active markets for stablecoins, with stablecoins accounting for approximately 80% of the declared cryptocurrency trading volume in Brazil in 2025. Users still open the familiar local app; the interface and brand haven't changed, only a US dollar settlement channel has quietly been added in the background. If you can't get a license, invest in those who do. The longer the pipeline, the more difficult it is to circumvent regulation. On June 30, 2024, the EU's MiCA stablecoin terms came into effect, and on December 30, MiCA was fully implemented. USDT did not obtain EU authorization, and licensed exchanges in Europe successively restricted or delisted its trading. Tether chose to circumvent this. In November, it stopped issuing the euro-denominated stablecoin EURT, instead supporting third-party projects in Europe and promoting its own tokenization platform, Hadron. In November 2024, it announced an investment in Quantoz, a Dutch central bank-licensed electronic money institution; in December, it invested in StablR, which issues compliant stablecoins EURR and USDR, both using Hadron. USDT couldn't enter Europe, but Tether's technology and capital did. In February of this year, it made a strategic investment of $100 million in Anchorage Digital, a US federally licensed crypto bank. Anchorage is the issuer of the US-compliant stablecoin USA₮, which launched on January 27th. USDT remains overseas, while USA₮ is issued by a licensed bank—two parallel lines. While the European and American markets require indirect investment, in Switzerland and Singapore, with their relatively open regulatory frameworks, Tether directly invests in licensed institutions. This week's signing of SCRYPT, which has been operating under the supervision of the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA) and the self-regulatory organization VQF since 2019, and MetaComp, which holds a major payment institution license from the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), will directly expand its compliance and cross-border channels. Rather than applying for licenses from scratch, Tether prefers to directly invest in institutions that already hold licenses. Tether is even looking towards non-human users. On October 15th, Tether Capital made a strategic investment in AIsa. On this platform, companies can set spending limits for AI agents, allowing them to purchase data, software, and computing power independently. Currently, the platform has over 250,000 agents and has processed over 100 million transactions. This type of small-amount, high-frequency, 24/7 machine settlement is difficult to process through traditional bank accounts, making stablecoins the most direct payment tool. A Payment Company That Doesn't Rely on Transaction Fees for Survival: Looking at Tether's investments from 2024 to 2026 reveals a fundamental difference in cost structure between Tether and traditional payment companies. Tether holds only minority stakes in most of its investment companies; Adecoagro, a Latin American agricultural company in which it holds approximately 74.8%, is a rare exception and has little to do with payments. Stripe, PayPal, and remittance companies around the world rely on transaction fees charged to merchants to cover operating costs and bad debts; transaction fees are their lifeblood. Tether's recurring profits come from US Treasury bonds and repurchase agreement interest. It doesn't need to take a cut from every payment; as long as USDT is actually used, its reserve size will increase accordingly. Therefore, it can exchange equity for channels or lower the barrier for partners to use USDT by paying money. In February 2025, Tether led a $3 million pre-seed round for MANSA. MANSA specifically uses USDT to provide pre-financing liquidity to payment companies, allowing them to complete cross-border settlements instantly without having to deposit large sums of money in various locations. Traditional channel providers have also seen this gap; Stripe has acquired the stablecoin infrastructure company Bridge to enter the market itself. However, Stripe is essentially a payment company that collects transaction fees, while Tether does not expect to make money from the payment process, so it is naturally more willing to offer lower fees. The switch is in someone else's hands. This approach also has its limitations. USDT has been delisted in Europe, and Ualá has yet to integrate it. In the US market, it can only be issued via USA₮. Tether can pay to become a shareholder, but it can't turn on the regulatory switch for different countries. The further the pipeline extends into licensed banks and payment institutions, the more it encounters the most sensitive capital controls, anti-money laundering regulations of sovereign states, and a dollar clearing network that bypasses the traditional bank correspondent banking system. Currently, central banks still regulate stablecoins as crypto assets. Once USDT truly flows into wages and loans, the regulatory standards will shift to systemically important financial infrastructure. The interest printing press is still running, but at a significantly slower pace. Every check Tether signs around the world has a clear purpose: to channel more real dollars into its pipeline. How much of this pipeline will ultimately function is not in Tether's hands.

data.title: Goldman Sachs 2027 Macro Outlook: Precious Metals Seem to Be Back to 2022
data.description:
This week's recent bloodbath in non-ferrous and precious metals is reminiscent of the fleeting beauty of a thousand miles in a single day. Interest rate hikes, AI-driven regulatory clearing under the blue wave, and deleveraging have made for a truly turbulent year-end market. Goldman Sachs' 2027 macroeconomic outlook has just been released, so let's see how they view precious metals.

■ For precious metals, 2027 is increasingly resembling 2022: rising Fed policy rates are suppressing private investor demand, but structural gold purchases by central banks are providing solid support for gold prices. Therefore, we believe there are short-term downside risks and increased volatility during the Fed's continued rate hikes, but with continued central bank gold purchases, we still expect gold prices to slowly climb to $4,650/ounce by the end of 2027. Once the Fed begins cutting interest rates, we expect demand for Western ETFs to rebound, pushing gold prices even stronger to $5,600/oz by the end of 2028. The baseline scenario carries significant upside risk if macroeconomic policies offset the return of demand. ■ The same 2022 scenario should favor gold over silver. Interest rate hikes suppress private investment demand for both metals, but only gold benefits from structural buying by central banks. Therefore, we expect gold to outperform silver in 2027 unless another silver liquidity squeeze occurs—which we believe is unsustainable given the Fed's rate hike cycle and pressure on silver ETF demand. ■ For platinum and palladium, continued uncertainty surrounding US tariffs should keep supply fragmented and volatility high, but does not necessarily mean higher prices in 2027. Interest rate hikes should suppress investment demand—especially for platinum, which accounts for a larger share of investment than palladium, while rising electric vehicle penetration remains a structural headwind for automotive demand. Platinum faces greater pressure as European fleets, which have a higher proportion of diesel vehicles, shift to electric vehicles; while palladium's demand decline in automotive catalysts should be more gradual due to the rising share of hybrid vehicles and a slower electrification transition in the US market, which has a higher proportion of gasoline vehicles. ■ In this 2027 outlook, we discuss our views on precious metals, key risks, and implications for investors in a Q&A format: we cover the upside and downside risks to our gold forecast, why gold failed to hedge against the 2026 Strait of Hormuz supply shock, how opportunities vary depending on investor horizons, why we expect central bank gold purchases to remain structural, and the risks of the People's Bank of China's gold purchases and potential official selling. We then turn to why we expect gold to outperform silver during the Fed's rate hike cycle, and why continued supply disruptions will cause platinum and palladium prices to fluctuate but not necessarily drive prices higher.

I. Gold: Structural Central Bank Support Amid Cyclical Interest Rate Headwinds

Question 1: What are your gold price forecasts for 2027 and beyond?

We maintain a constructive view on gold in the long term, based on structurally strong central bank gold purchases (including by the People's Bank of China), but given the Fed's hawkish outlook, we believe the short-term environment is more challenging.

Our economists expect a third 25 basis point rate hike in March 2027, following the anticipated second rate hike in December 2026, suppressing demand for interest rate-sensitive Western ETFs.

Nevertheless, we expect continued central bank gold purchases to push gold prices to $4,650 by the end of 2027, a 19% increase from the spot price and a 13% increase from the October average (Figures 1 & 2).

The Fed's recent hawkish shift and rising policy rates should also dampen investors' "currency devaluation concerns."

Therefore, we assume that macroeconomic policy hedging demand for gold—reflected in call option demand—will revert to its historical average (Figure 3). We expect private investor demand (reflected through demand for interest rate-sensitive Western ETFs) to eventually rebound after four 25-basis-point rate cuts between November 2027 and September 2028, bringing the federal funds rate down to a terminal rate of 3.25%–3.5%, thereby removing interest rate constraints on gold prices and supporting a rise to $5,600/oz by the end of 2028 (Figure 1). Figure 1: We forecast gold to be at $4,650/oz by the end of 2027 and $5,600/oz by the end of 2028. Figure 2: We maintain our long-term constructive view on strong structural central bank demand – which drives most of our projected price upside to the end of 2027. Starting from an October average of $4,100/oz, we believe the recent price weakness is primarily driven by speculative positioning and may therefore prove temporary.

Figure 3: We expect macroeconomic policy hedging demand for gold—reflected in call option demand and potentially a key amplifier of the 2025/early 2026 rally—to further retreat to historical levels.

We believe the 2027 landscape will resemble 2022 (Figure 4): central banks will provide strong structural buying, but higher federal funds rates will suppress investor positioning, resulting in a more moderate net increase in gold prices.

Figure 4: The current situation is similar to 2022: Central banks provide strong structural buying, but higher interest rates suppress investor positioning. **Question 2: What risks do you face in your gold forecast?** We believe a more hawkish Fed stance poses further downside risks in the short term. In a scenario with four rate hikes and higher terminal rates (Figure 6), we estimate gold prices to be $4,585/oz by the end of 2027 (red dashed line in Figure 5). Larger ETF selling could further depress prices. The significant increase in gold ETF holdings over the past three years reflects a normal upward trend driven by lower interest rates, investor wealth growth (captured by our interest rate-implied autoregressive ETF model), and the potential boost from recent depreciation trades. We expect two additional Fed rate hikes to eliminate the latter, but cannot clearly distinguish it from structural wealth trends. As a conservative lower bound, we therefore assume that all ETF holdings exceeding the level implied by interest rates alone will be reduced, implying an additional 300 tons of selling, with the gold price at $4,265/oz by the end of 2027 (grey dashed line in Figure 5, Figure 7). Figure 5: Higher terminal interest rates and ETF sell-offs pose downside risks to our baseline scenario (US$4,650/oz by the end of 2027). Figure 6: Our US economists project a rate hike in December 2026 and another in March 2027; further rate hikes and higher terminal interest rates pose downside risks to our gold price forecast. Figure 7: A more hawkish Fed could—in extreme scenarios—drive a reduction of 300 tons of gold ETF holdings.

There are also tactical downside risks surrounding our fair value forecast. Our forecast captures the slower-moving drivers of gold prices, namely demand from Western ETFs and central banks, but speculative positioning could temporarily deviate prices from fair value. COMEX speculative positioning is already at a low 45th percentile, and we expect it to rebound in the baseline scenario. That said, rising oil prices could trigger further systemic CTA selling, while a sharp pullback in equities (e.g., related to AI cycle uncertainty) could initially drag gold lower as margin calls and broader deleveraging force investors to raise cash (Figure 8).

Figure 8: Intraday, rising oil prices suppressed gold through systemic selling, while the sharp stock market pullback initially suppressed it through deleveraging. In the long term, if macroeconomic policy hedging demand returns after the Fed begins cutting rates, we believe there is significant upside potential beyond the baseline scenario. Perceived fiscal sustainability concerns in Western economies, potentially exacerbated by increased military spending and rising debt burdens in energy-importing countries, could revive this macroeconomic policy hedging demand if investors also begin to worry about how developed market central banks will respond. Once lower interest rates remove the ceiling on gold price increases, the potential resurgence of fiscal sustainability concerns could push gold prices significantly beyond our baseline scenario of $5,600/oz by the end of 2028. Question 3: Gold did not rise despite rising inflation during the 2026 Strait of Hormuz impact. Has gold's role as an inflation hedge or safe-haven asset changed? We believe not. We have long argued that gold is not a universally applicable stagflation hedge because the source of inflation is crucial. There are two distinct stagflation scenarios in which stock-bond portfolios typically underperform, and gold performs differently in each. The first scenario is characterized by growing market concerns about institutional credibility. When markets doubt central banks' willingness or ability to curb inflation, inflation can spike, causing both bonds and stocks to fall. The 1970s are a prime example: US fiscal expansion and the loss of Federal Reserve independence fueled runaway inflation, and gold surged as investors sought a store of value outside the system. The second scenario involves supply disruptions that simultaneously weaken growth and drive up prices, such as in 2022 when Russia (which then supplied 40% of Europe's gas) cut supply. Commodities—as disrupted inputs—are among the few assets with positive real returns. As in 2022, gold typically underperforms initially in supply disruption events. Supply-driven inflation increases the risk of monetary policy tightening, rising yields increase the opportunity cost of holding gold and suppress ETF demand, while potential stock market pullbacks trigger margin-related liquidations. The 2026 Strait of Hormuz shock falls into the second scenario, as the inflationary shock originates from disrupted commodity supplies. Question 4: What advice do you have for investors? ■ The next 3-6 months may remain challenging for CTAs and macro hedge funds: rising federal funds rates in our baseline scenario, high uncertainty in energy prices, volatility from inflation and labor market data, and strict drawdown limits all make maintaining long positions difficult. Higher oil prices could add pressure through systemic selling, while a sharp stock market pullback could initially drag gold lower as margin calls and broader deleveraging force investors to raise cash. ■ However, for long-term investors seeking exposure to rising central bank demand and/or tail risks in macroeconomic policy (i.e., gold as a "depreciation" hedge), the current gold price pullback may offer a more attractive entry point. Structural central bank demand remains supportive, and private wealth and other long-term investors may value gold as insurance against fiscal sustainability risks in developed markets, even if these risks are not realized in our baseline scenario.

Question 5: Central bank demand is a key pillar of your gold outlook. Why do you believe this demand is structural and expect continued gold purchases?

Our view of strong structural central bank demand drives most of our projected price upside through the end of 2027 (60 tonnes per month from 2026–2028, compared to an average of 17 tonnes per month before 2022).

Although the seasonally adjusted 3-month moving average fell to 51 tonnes per month in September from 85 tonnes per month in August, we expect gold purchases to have resumed as prices subsequently stabilized, thus placing greater emphasis on the previously stronger months (Figure 9). Figure 9: Our Goldman Sachs immediate forecast for central bank gold purchases fell to the seasonally adjusted 3-month baseline of 51 tonnes per month in September, down from 85 tonnes per month in August (compared to the pre-2022 average of 17 tonnes per month). Since the freezing of Russian reserves in 2022, central banks—especially emerging market central banks—have accelerated their gold purchases by approximately five times. We view this as a structural shift in reserve management behavior and do not expect it to reverse in the short term. Our baseline scenario assumes that the current cumulative trend in the official sector continues for another three years. Our rationale is that emerging market central banks' gold allocations remain significantly lower than their developed market counterparts, and the motivation to diversify away from G7 reserve currencies (including geopolitical and financial risks) may still exist. For example, we estimate that China—the largest buyer—holds approximately 11.8% of its reserves in gold, compared to approximately 80% for the US, Germany, France, and Italy (Figure 11). The global average is over 20%, which we consider a reasonable medium-term target for large emerging market central banks, based on historical precedent, current allocations, and our communications with emerging market central bank reserve managers. For example, Russia increased its gold holdings from 8% to 20% between 2014 and 2020 and repatriated its gold reserves before sanctions. If the largest official buyer—China—targets a 20% allocation and maintains an average purchase pace of approximately 20 tonnes per month (consistent with its 12-month moving average) (Figure 10), we estimate it would take approximately three years to reach a 20% gold holding. Our estimates also take into account the potential for continued global central bank gold purchases (60 tonnes/month) to push up gold prices over time—thus increasing the nominal value of existing holdings and helping to reach allocation targets more quickly (see Appendix for details). A recent World Gold Council survey supports our view: of the 76 central banks surveyed between February and May 2026, a record 45% expect to increase their own gold reserves in the next 12 months—the highest percentage since the survey began in 2018—while approximately 90% expect global reserves to rise, with the remainder expecting holdings to remain largely stable. Question 6: Will China's gold allocation eventually exceed your reasonable 20% target? Yes. We believe there is upside risk to China's 20% gold allocation target, as larger gold reserves could support the internationalization of the renminbi. The path for a currency to become a more important international currency generally involves three steps: increased use in third-party trade, increased role in international bond markets, and ultimately, its establishment in the reserves of other countries. While the first two steps are already underway, the final step is typically the harvest stage for any emerging reserve currency, as reserve managers seek to diversify from the existing reserve system while also considering the asset composition supporting the alternative currency. History suggests that gold can help complete this transition: as a reserve asset independent of any issuer's credit or political stance, gold can enhance confidence in an international currency. After World War II, substantial gold holdings helped support confidence that the US dollar had surpassed the British pound as the dominant reserve currency, reinforcing the notion that the currency was "as reliable as gold." Therefore, regardless of whether an emerging currency ultimately achieves dominant reserve status, gold accumulation can be part of a strategy, suggesting that China's desired gold allocation may eventually exceed 20%. Question 7: Reports indicate that the Turkish central bank has sold off a large amount of reserves since the outbreak of the Middle East conflict. Will central bank gold sales expand? We believe a broader central bank gold sell-off is unlikely—our immediate forecasts actually show a rebound in central bank gold purchases since May—and even the reported decline from Turkey may overstate the actual sell-off. Turkey's reserve reporting method is unusual because gold swaps can show a decline in reported gold reserves even if the gold is not directly sold, which may explain in part the 129-ton drop at the beginning of the Middle East conflict and its subsequent rapid rebound (Figure 12). Figure 12: Data from the Turkish Central Bank shows that gold reserves rebounded after a drop of 129 tons at the beginning of the Middle East conflict. More fundamentally, Turkey is an exception: as an emerging market central bank, it faces potential foreign exchange liquidity needs, and its unusually high allocation of over 60% of its foreign exchange reserves to gold makes gold (swaps) a more natural source of liquidity than most emerging market reserve managers (who typically hold well below 20%). Only a few countries share this characteristic: Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan also have unusually high gold allocations, while Russia and Venezuela face more specific restrictions on other reserve assets, similarly making gold a more natural source of liquidity. Therefore, we view these countries as more likely exceptions to gold swaps or sell-offs, rather than signals of a broader sell-off by emerging market central banks. We are skeptical of concerns that Gulf states might also sell off their gold reserves. The proportion of gold in the Gulf states' reserves is significantly lower. Gold accounts for approximately 4% of the UAE's reserves, 8% of Saudi Arabia's, 5% of Oman's, and about 24% of Qatar's, compared to over 60% of Turkey's foreign exchange reserves (Figure 13)—an unusually high proportion for an emerging market economy. Gulf economies typically peg to the US dollar, meaning that foreign exchange intervention is more likely to be carried out by selling US Treasury bonds rather than gold. The Gulf's reserve structure reduces the likelihood that its central banks would liquidate gold for foreign exchange management purposes. Figure 13: Turkey's proportion of gold in its foreign exchange reserves is significantly higher than that of the Gulf states. Question 8: Will developed market central banks holding large legacy gold reserves become sellers? We believe this risk is currently small. If anything, interest in gold and reserve security is expanding beyond emerging market central banks. Since 2022, developed market central banks have largely remained on the sidelines of the gold-buying spree, partly because they already hold substantial gold reserves for historical reasons, typically dispersed across domestic and international custodians, particularly the Bank of England and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, to manage jurisdictional, political, and physical risks. Concerns about geopolitical instability were one reason some European central banks moved some of their gold reserves to New York during the Cold War. However, feedback from developed market central banks suggests the discussion is increasingly shifting from whether to hold gold to where to store it: for example, France and the Netherlands have recently made repeated moves to move their gold reserves out of New York. This greater focus on reserve security indicates that developed market reserve managers are increasingly considering the tail risks that initially give gold its strategic value, reinforcing the rationale for holding rather than selling it.

II. Silver: The Run Ends, But the Fed Continues to Raise Rates

Question 9: Silver had an extraordinary start to the year, peaking above $120/oz with extreme price volatility. Do you expect a repeat in 2027?

Our baseline scenario is no. The silver rally in 2025/26 reflects an unusual combination of rising investor demand and tight liquidity in London, which we do not expect to be repeated during the Fed's rate hike cycle (Figure 14).

Figure 14: Silver peaked in early 2026 due to a clash between rising investor demand and tight liquidity in London. Speculation surrounding US trade policy—silver being included on the critical minerals list, and therefore theoretically eligible for tariffs even if exempted in April 2025—encouraged the pre-shipment of the metal to the US in 2025, drawing inventories away from London, which sets global benchmark prices. As London inventories dwindled, strong investor flows—supported by Fed rate cuts, silver chasing gold, and spillover effects from devaluation trades—absorbed an increasingly larger share of the remaining available metal, ultimately triggering a liquidity squeeze (Figure 15). While a weekly net demand of 1,000 tonnes of silver typically boosts prices by about 2%, we estimate that price sensitivity rises to about 7% during a run. As investor demand subsequently weakens and tensions ease, prices fall sharply. Figure 15: Tariff concerns draw silver to the US, draining London inventories; subsequent surge in investor demand absorbs the remaining silver, disproportionately impacting prices. We believe a repeat of the 2025/26 run in 2027 is unlikely: even if new tariff concerns again draw silver from London to the US, a Fed rate hike in early 2027 should suppress ETF demand, eliminating the second leg of the 2025/26 run. Once the Fed resumes its easing policies, surging ETF demand could push silver prices higher again, but another liquidity crunch in London could require renewed tariff concerns and a restart of US inventory accumulation. Question 10: Is the gold-silver ratio still worth watching? Will silver outperform gold again as the ratio returns to near the top of its historical range? No, we believe gold may outperform silver again in 2027, at least during the Fed's rate hike cycle. Like gold—investment demand is the primary driver of silver prices. Historically, private investment flows in the gold and silver markets have moved in tandem (Figure 16), keeping the gold-silver ratio within a wide range of 45-80 (Figure 17). Figure 16: Key Drivers of Silver and Gold – Private Investment Flows – Moving in Tandem… However, since 2022, gold has decoupled from its price, driven by a surge in central bank purchases, pushing up prices even without private investment inflows. Silver, lacking central bank buying, has lagged behind. Figure 17: ...The gold-silver price ratio remained within a wide range of 45-80 before gold decoupled due to central bank gold purchases in 2022. The 2025/26 London silver liquidity squeeze temporarily reversed this divergence, pushing silver prices sharply higher and the gold-silver ratio to the bottom of its historical range. As the squeeze subsided, the gold-silver ratio returned to the top of its range, but we do not believe this signals a return to silver outperforming. Fed rate hikes should suppress private investment demand for both metals, but gold has retained structural buying from central banks. Given that another silver liquidity squeeze during a rate hike cycle is unlikely (see Question 9), we expect gold to outperform silver again in 2027, at least until the Fed resumes its accommodative stance.

III. Platinum and Palladium: Still Segmented

Question 11: Platinum and palladium remain under the US Section 232 tariff investigation. What does this mean for the outlook?

We believe the main risks are continued supply segmentation and volatility stemming from ongoing uncertainty surrounding US tariffs (Figure 18), but we believe actual US tariffs on platinum and palladium are unlikely.

Figure 18: US Tariff Risks Since 2025 Drive Platinum and Palladium Supply Segmentation, Exacerbating Volatility and Run Risk

Platinum and palladium are key inputs, especially for the automotive industry, but global supply is unusually concentrated: Southern Africa accounts for approximately 82%/46% of platinum/palladium supply, and Russia accounts for another 11%/39%—creating a significant risk of disruption.

Reducing reliance on foreign supplies of key minerals and rebuilding domestic capacity appear to be increasingly important policy objectives for the United States. Theoretically, tariffs are one way to achieve this policy objective: making imported minerals more expensive, protecting domestic producers, and ultimately incentivizing investment in U.S. mines, smelters, and refineries. In practice, the supply response to platinum group metals is limited. Domestic U.S. mineral production is limited, expanding output is technically and geologically challenging, and new mines and refineries take years to be approved, built, and put into operation. Because tariffs change much faster than capacity building, the resulting policy uncertainty could undermine the long-term investment it is intended to encourage. However, tariff risks can still achieve national security objectives by attracting metal inventories to the U.S. without large-scale government purchases or immediately raising costs for downstream consumers. The result is reduced liquidity outside the U.S.—leading to price volatility—even if global inventories appear ample on paper. Question 12: Does continued supply disruption mean higher platinum and palladium prices in 2027? Not necessarily. Supply disruptions keep volatility risks high, but the demand landscape in 2027 is more complex. Fed rate hikes should suppress investment demand, particularly for platinum, which accounts for a larger share of investment than palladium. The electric vehicle transition should also continue to reduce demand for platinum group metals, although the impact may differ for the two metals. Platinum faces greater headwinds from European electric vehicles, but also gains more upside potential due to defense spending. Historically, Europe has had a higher proportion of diesel vehicles, making its fleet relatively more reliant on platinum. Therefore, the rising penetration rate of electric vehicles has a particularly significant impact on platinum demand. Our automotive analyst report states that in August 2026, sales of pure electric vehicles in Europe increased by 66% year-on-year, while implied sales of internal combustion engines decreased by 10% year-on-year. However, military vehicles remain highly dependent on diesel, making higher defense spending a potential offsetting factor. Palladium receives more support from hybrid vehicles and the slower US electric vehicle transition. Gasoline vehicles are more reliant on palladium, while hybrid vehicle growth supports palladium demand, as hybrid vehicles are primarily gasoline-powered. In the US, pure electric vehicle sales declined by 45% year-on-year in Q3 2026, while hybrid vehicle sales increased by 27% year-on-year. This suggests that demand for gasoline-powered catalysts may persist longer as the share of hybrid vehicles increases and the adoption of pure electric vehicles slows.
